terms.gloss: the gullet, the passage food and drink go down
evidence: Plin. NH 11.176: gula, quā cibus atque pōtus dēvolant
Plin. NH 11.179: summum gulae faucēs vocantur, extremum stomachus
terms.comment: Pliny’s word for the gullet: the windpipe and the gullet are the two passages of the neck, and the gullet runs to the stomach (NH 11.176); its top is the faucēs (see throat). It is also the throat or neck as one is seized by it (obtortā gulā, Cic. Verr. 2.4.24), and very often gluttony (see glutton). The anatomists’ term is Oesophagus (Terminologia Anatomica), from Greek οἰσοφάγος; Morgan–Owens gives oesophagus from a work of 1811 beside stomachus (M-O s.v. oesophagus).

terms.gloss: the gullet (the word’s first sense, in anatomy)
evidence: Cels. 4.1.3: alterum asperam artēriam nōminant, alterum stomachum
Cic. ND 2.135: linguam autem ad rādīcēs ejus haerēns excipit stomachus
terms.comment: The word of Celsus and of Cicero’s account of the body for the gullet; Celsus does not use gula. In everyday Latin stomachus is the stomach (see stomach), so gula is the clearer word for the gullet.

phrases.latin: altera exterior appellētur sānē gula, quā cibus atque pōtus dēvolant.
phrases.english: the other, the outer one, may fairly be called the gullet: food and drink go down it.

phrases.latin: Artēria exterior ad pulmōnem, stomachus interior ad ventriculum fertur; illa spīritum, hic cibum recipit.
phrases.english: The windpipe, in front, runs to the lung, the gullet, behind it, to the stomach; the one takes in breath, the other food.

sources: Lewis & Short: gula · Lewis & Short: stomachus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 58, 310.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. oesophagus.
